opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely one of the hardest forecasting problems we've ever faced, and I try to hold my predictions pretty loosely. Part of the difficulty is that the technology itself is moving so fast — the capabilities we have today would have seemed implausible to most people even a few years ago, so any forecast that assumes a static baseline is almost certainly wrong.

But the deeper issue is that the second-order effects are where most of the transformation actually happens, and those are notoriously hard to see in advance. If you go back to the early days of the internet, plenty of people correctly predicted that information would become cheaper to distribute. Far fewer predicted social media, the gig economy, or how it would reshape politics. I think AI is like that, but probably more so, because it's not just a new channel for information — it's a general-purpose technology that touches cognition itself.

So the way I think about it is: be fairly confident about the direction of a few first-order trends — things like the cost of certain kinds of cognitive work dropping dramatically — and be very humble about how institutions, labor markets, and people's behavior will adapt in response. And I think that humility actually has a practical implication, especially for those of us building in this space. It means we should invest heavily in understanding these systems — what's actually happening inside the models, why they behave the way they do — because if we can't predict the societal effects with confidence, we at least want to be able to see clearly what the technology is doing and steer it as things unfold.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI capabilities changing rapidly while saying societal effects, especially second-order changes and adaptations, are difficult to predict. It distinguishes confidence in a few broad trends from humility about the full transformation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think the first thing to admit is that we're bad at this, and we've always been bad at it. Go back and look at what people said when the internet was taking off. The smartest people in the room got the broad direction right and almost every specific wrong. Nobody drew a line from TCP/IP to Instagram influencers or to a global ride-hailing market. The technology was knowable. The second-order effects on how people actually live were not.

AI feels harder than that to me, for a couple of reasons. One is that it's a general capability rather than a single product. Electricity is probably the better analogy than the smartphone. You don't predict electricity by asking what the lightbulb does. You have to ask what happens when every other industry gets rebuilt around the assumption that it exists, and that took decades to play out.

The second reason is that the usual tool we reach for, extrapolation, keeps breaking. We've been surprised on the capability curve repeatedly, in both directions. Things we thought were far off arrived early, and things we assumed would be trivial, like reliability in long-horizon tasks, turned out to be stubborn. So if you can't even forecast the technology eighteen months out with confidence, forecasting the societal response on top of that is compounding uncertainty on uncertainty.

And then there's the part people underweight, which is that society isn't a passive recipient. Institutions push back, regulation shows up, norms shift, people adapt in ways that look irrational from the outside. Adoption is a human process and humans are slow and weird. So the gap between what's technically possible and what actually changes can stay open for a long time, and then close very suddenly.

So how do I think about it practically? I've mostly given up trying to predict specific outcomes and instead try to identify which bets are robust across a wide range of futures. Where is the cost of being wrong asymmetric? What would I regret not having built, or not having paid attention to, in most of the plausible worlds? That's a less satisfying answer than a prediction, but I think the people who confidently tell you exactly what 2035 looks like are mostly telling you about themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says AI’s societal effects are hard to forecast and may unfold suddenly, but it does not clearly state that expecting rapid AI-driven change still leaves the full range of social transformations unpredictable.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s difficult because you’re trying to predict both what the technology will be capable of and how people will respond to it. And those two things interact. A capability becomes available, people find unexpected uses for it, institutions adapt, and that changes what gets built next.

Even if you knew exactly how capable AI would be five years from now, you still wouldn’t know exactly how society would look. You’d need to understand how quickly organizations adopt it, what people trust it to do, and where they decide they still want a human involved.

So I tend to think in terms of possible scenarios rather than one precise forecast. What changes across a wide range of outcomes? Which assumptions are doing the most work? And what could we observe today that would tell us we need to update our view? You can take the potential for enormous change seriously while being humble about its shape and timing.

r001.rationale: The response takes the potential for enormous AI-driven change seriously while saying society’s resulting shape and timing remain hard to predict, including because people and institutions respond in unexpected ways.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s difficult because you’re trying to predict two things at once: how the technology will develop, and how people and institutions will respond to it. Even if you could forecast the capabilities pretty accurately, that wouldn’t tell you how quickly organizations will adopt them, which tasks people will delegate, or what new things they’ll decide to do.

So I try to think in terms of scenarios rather than one confident prediction. What changes if progress is faster or slower? What assumptions would have to hold? And what decisions make sense across several possible futures? You can take the potential for enormous change seriously while still being humble about its timing and shape.

r001.rationale: The response says major change is possible and its timing and shape are uncertain, but it does not state that expecting rapid AI-driven change fails to predict the full range of societal transformations.
